text: The two helpers are published as versioned platform library artefacts pinned by the service template, together with the rest of the shared library baseline of RWB-PLT-NF02-APP.
why: Architecture v5 slide 20 puts every service on the service template and the shared libraries, and N009 is a platform key with no service of its own, so the helper must reach the 19 services through one pinned set; no source names the package, the registry or the version label of that set.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 20 (every service from the service template and the shared libraries); Change Register v1 N009 row; RWB-PLT-NF02-APP sections 3 and 13 (one baseline release, one pin in the template)
confirm: Platform team at the wave 0 baseline review
impact: Names the distribution of the helper and the pin only; no rule, no business value and no service path changes

text: The idempotency store is the idempotency_key table of RWB-PLT-TE006-CON applied in each service's own schema, so the helper creates no table of its own.
why: The Ownership Map keeps idempotency_key with PLT as a library object created in every service schema, and Architecture v5 slide 29 forbids a cross-schema write; the implementation cannot place the stored response without that ruling.
read: Ownership Map v1 idempotency_key row (owner PLT, library object created in every service schema); RWB-PLT-TE006-CON section 12.7 (the DDL template applied by each service's own Flyway sequence); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 20 and 29
confirm: ACE DBA and platform team at the wave 0 design gate
impact: The stored response is written in the calling service's own schema; the helper adds no table, no column and no schema

text: The error map is a data file shipped with the library, keyed by message code, holding the HTTP status and the problem type, and never a literal in service code.
why: Architecture v5 slide 11 fixes RFC 9457 problem details but names no store of the mapping from a message code to a status and a type, while the message codes belong to the message catalogue; a shipped data file is the only read that keeps a new code out of nineteen code bases.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 11 (RFC 9457 problem details on every error) and slide 20 (template and shared libraries); Ownership Map v1; RWB-PLT-N009-CON section 13 (error map columns)
confirm: Message-catalogue owner and platform team at the contract freeze
impact: The map is data; a new message code is a map row and a library release, not a code change in a service

text: The header is Idempotency-Key, case-insensitive, and a stored response is scoped to the service, the operation and the key; the expiry window is a chart value and its default is not specified — the working read is the platform default recorded at the wave 0 review.
why: Architecture v5 slide 11 requires an Idempotency-Key on every POST and a stored response per key, and names neither the header format, nor the scope tuple, nor the expiry window; the contract cannot be published without a read, and the scope must not be guessed per service.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 11 (Idempotency-Key on every POST; Duplicates, order: a stored response); Ownership Map v1; RWB-PLT-TE006-CON section 12.7 (idempotency_key with the unique key on scope and key)
confirm: Platform team at the wave 0 review and the API review at the contract freeze
impact: Fixes the header name, the scope tuple and the expiry rule; the header format and the default window stay open until the review

text: The local decision record is written in the caller's own schema by a library object owned by PLT, and the central ledger decision_log_entry in rwb_decision is P7's; the library never writes another service's table and never writes the ledger.
why: Architecture v5 slide 20 puts decision_record in every service's own schema and slide 28 keeps the ledger in rwb-decision, while no source publishes a DDL for the local table or states whether the chain is one per schema or one per instance.
read: Architecture v5 slides 20, 28, 29 and 41; Temporal and Drools Design slide 16; Ownership Map row decision_log_entry owner P7; CG-B-PLT-LIB-01-E1027-1
confirm: Solution architect
impact: Every service's DB story applies the template in its own schema; P7 owns the ledger, the ingest and the chain check; no foreign key crosses a service boundary

text: The library keeps the legacy interface behaviour: the write is @Transactional(propagation = MANDATORY), a refusal names the missing field with MSG-P7-009 and a failed append raises with MSG-P7-003, the same idempotency key gives one record with the repeat counted, and the record carries the seven field groups of the legacy story.
why: The legacy story fixes the interface and the seven field groups and the target documents fix only the split of the table and the transport; no source republishes the interface or renumbers the messages.
read: RWB-E1-027 sections 4, 8, 12 and 14; Architecture v5 slide 28; Temporal and Drools Design slide 16; CG-B-PLT-LIB-01-E1027-1
confirm: Solution architect
impact: The writer interface, the refusal and failure shapes and the repeat metric stay stable for the wave 1 callers and for the ITG proof; the incident route is each service's own alerting

text: The DecisionRecorded record key is caseId where the record has a case and the entry id where it does not, so an access event with no case still announces its record in an order the ledger can correlate.
why: Architecture v5 slide 22 and Template and Rules R4 fix caseId as the record key and the legacy story keys the event on the event identifier, but no source states the key of a record with no case.
read: Architecture v5 slides 20, 22 and 28; Template and Rules R4; RWB-E1-027 section 12; CG-B-PLT-LIB-01-E1027-1
confirm: Solution architect
impact: The P7 ingest accepts both keys; the access-event writer of P4 rwb-access publishes under the entry id

text: The contract is published as one versioned artefact with major version 1, consumed as a pinned version by every service, and carries the record columns named on the Temporal and Drools Design slide 16 plus the decision code, the case, the actor and the idempotency key of the legacy story.
why: No source publishes the record schema, the local table DDL, the envelope payload schema or the message catalogue entry of MSG-P7-009 and MSG-P7-003, so the contract's own v1 is the only specification the consuming stories can build and test against.
read: Temporal and Drools Design slide 16; Architecture v5 slides 20, 22 and 28; Template and Rules R4 and R7.2; RWB-E1-027 sections 11, 12 and 14; CG-B-PLT-LIB-01-E1027-2
confirm: Solution architect
impact: The record shape, the DDL template and the envelope freeze at v1; the table shape and the payload schema carry the gap reference until a published specification exists

text: The event name is rwb.decision.DecisionRecorded.v1 by the Template and Rules R4 naming rule, while the topic keeps the shared name rwb.decision-record.v1 that R4 fixes for all 19 producers.
why: R4 fixes both the shared topic and the event naming pattern, and the two do not derive from one another for a shared topic, so the event name is taken from the pattern and the topic name from the shared-topic row.
read: Template and Rules R4 (shared topic rwb.decision-record.v1; event names rwb.<short>.<Event>.v1); Architecture v5 slides 20 and 42 (DecisionRecorded produced by all 19); CG-B-PLT-LIB-01-E1027-2
confirm: Solution architect
impact: The registry subject and the schema entry of the event follow the event name; the topic ACLs follow the shared topic; the integration harness consumes the same pair

text: Authorisation stays with the owning service: the library validates the action, asks the access owner and fails closed, and the object-level decision is the service's own.
why: Architecture v5 slide 10 gives each service the object-level decision from cached rwb-access data and names OWASP API1 object-level authorisation; a shared library that decided the object itself would move the decision away from the service that holds the record and would break the per-service rule of slide 35.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 10 (each service authorises the object itself, OWASP API1, 2 s timeouts, breaker per downstream) and slide 35 (role, scope and DoA checked on every action from rwb-access data); slide 29 (deny by default)
confirm: Security architecture review at the contract freeze
impact: Fixes that the library asks and refuses and never decides the object; no business value changes

text: The permission and masking policy is cached per service, with the time to live read through the parameters client and refreshed on the two access events, so that no service reads a P4 table.
why: Slide 20 requires the two access events for cache refresh and slide 10 requires cached permission data from rwb-access; no source fixes the interval or the parameter key, and a per-service cache is the only shape that satisfies both without a cross-schema read under DP-01.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 10 (cached permission data from rwb-access) and slide 20 (AccessPolicyChanged, DoaLimitChanged to cache refresh); Template and Rules section R5.5 DP-01 and DP-06 (parameters contract and client library)
confirm: Platform review and the parameters catalog owner at the wave 0 gate
impact: Names the cache, its interval and its key only; the guard and masking outcomes of section 7 do not change

text: The masker fills from the value the data owner supplies and never from a token; with no rule the field is masked; id_no_last4 is the clearest identity value the library may hold.
why: ADR-010 and D-RCV-35 U1 remove tokenization and keep the clear identity number inside ACE, and the legacy story states the same rule for the view columns, so the library has no token path and no clear-identity path at all.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-037 sections 4, 8 (BR6, BR10) and 17; ADR-010; Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 35 (personal data masked before it leaves, no personal data in events or payloads)
confirm: Compliance and the data owner at the masking review (DL26)
impact: Fixes the source of every filled value; no masking value is chosen by this story

text: The authorise, permission and masking-policy operations are reached at /api/recovery/access/v1/... under the Template and Rules section R4 base, because Architecture v5 slide 14 names the operations and the Ownership Map has no path row for them.
why: Every consumed call needs a base; section R4 gives each service /api/recovery/<short>/v1 and the owner is P4 rwb-access; with no base the contract would have no reachable path, and the old monolith base is prohibited by DP-13.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 14 (POST /authorise, GET /me/permissions, GET /doa-limits, /masking-policies); Template and Rules section R4 (REST base /api/recovery/<short>/v1; DP-13); Ownership Map v1 api rows (no entry for the three operations)
confirm: API review at the contract freeze
impact: Fixes the three consumed paths only; no new path and no new service short is invented

text: The guard and masker are published as one versioned library artefact with major version 1, its contract shapes and its fakes, pinned by the service template.
why: The contract has to be frozen before nineteen services build against it, the template pins one version of the shared libraries, and a major version with published fakes is the only way a service can build and test before the access owner exists.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 20 and 38 (every service from the service template and the shared libraries); RWB-PLT-NF02-APP (one baseline version pinned, drift fails the build); Template and Rules section R5.7 rule 1
confirm: Platform library team and the service template owner at the wave 0 design gate
impact: Names the version and the pin only; the interface content of section 12 does not change

text: The catalog, the value versions and the five operations stay with P3 rwb-case under the R-PREC default ruling; the library only reads them through the published contract and holds no copy.
why: Template and Rules section R3 puts parameters and reference data (E1-042, E1-043) with rwb-case and DP-06 names the rwb-case parameters contract as the dependency; no source gives the platform library a schema, a store or a REST base, so a library that held the catalog would invent a service identity for itself.
read: Template and Rules section R3 default ruling and section R5.5 DP-06; Ownership Map tables parameter_catalog and parameter_value (owner P3) and api rows GET /admin/parameters, POST /admin/reference-loads, POST /admin/reference-loads/{loadId}/approve, POST /admin/reference-loads/{loadId}/verify and POST /admin/reference-loads/{loadId}/rollback (owner P3, ruling ASM-A6-api-4); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 14, 20 and 29

text: The client keeps the legacy behaviour: a typed read that answers the value with its version number and resolves the business date, the product group and the environment; a cache refreshed on the owner's approval event and otherwise by its time to live; and a start-up refusal when a required value has no value for the environment.
why: The legacy story fixes that behaviour in its flow and criteria and the realignment changes the storage, not the behaviour (U2); without this default the contract would have to invent a new semantics for a reader that 19 services already depend on.
read: RWB-E1-042 section 4 steps 1 to 9, section 5 X3 and X10, section 7 AC1, AC4, AC8, AC9 and AC11, section 12 (published interface, ParameterValue members) and section 13 (ParameterService, cache, ParameterStartupCheck)
applied_in: RWB-PLT-E1042-APP sections 2, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 13; RWB-PLT-E1042-CON sections 2, 7 and 12.4

impact: The semantics of every read in the 19 services; no value and no table changes

text: The two build checks stay with the library and are applied by the service template: RwbMagicNumberCheck allows 0, 1, -1 and test code and names the catalog key whose default equals the literal, and CatalogCompletenessCheck compares the keys read with the catalog file and fails on a missing key, owner or default.
why: The legacy story describes both checks in prose and places them in the monolith's build tools; in the target a check that fails a service's build cannot be owned by the owner of the catalog, and nineteen copies of the rule would drift.
read: RWB-E1-042 section 4 steps 2 and 3, section 5 X1 and X2, section 7 AC2 and AC3, section 13 (RwbMagicNumberCheck and CatalogCompletenessCheck in build-tools/rwb-checks) and section 17

confirm: Platform team at the pipeline review of the template
impact: Which builds fail and on what finding shape; no business rule changes

text: The approval event keeps the legacy name and travels as rwb.case.ParameterVersionApproved.v1 on the owner's topic rwb.case.events.v1 by section R4 naming.
why: Legacy section 12 calls the event ParameterVersionApproved and names no topic, while section R4 fixes rwb.<short>.<Event>.v1 on rwb.<short>.events.v1; the owner is rwb-case, so the name follows from the ruling and no source states it.

why: No source defines a published contract artefact for the client or its compatibility rule, and nineteen services cannot build against prose; the platform pattern of DP-11 requires a published contract with a mock before code.
read: RWB-E1-042 section 12 (published interface and response members); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 11 (contracts published before code, contract tests in every build and DP-11); Template and Rules section R5.5 DP-11

text: The environment name, the cache time to live and the catalog file are chart values and the time to live is itself a catalog entry: the chart holds RWB_ENV, RWB_PARAMETER_CATALOG and RWB_PARAMETER_TTL_KEY plus a bootstrap value that is compared with refdata.cache.ttl-seconds at deployment, and from the first catalog answer the catalog entry governs.
why: The legacy story requires a value change with no release and makes the cache time to live a catalog entry, while a cache cannot ask the catalog for its own time to live before it has read anything; the split between a bootstrap value and the governing entry is the only reading that satisfies both.
read: RWB-E1-042 section 3 (refdata.cache.ttl-seconds default 300, 30 in SIT), section 4 step 8 and section 13 (cache time to live as a catalog entry; config.cache.ttl-seconds = 60 assumed; DL11); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 38 (one Helm chart and the golden pipeline in wave 0)
confirm: Platform team and the DevOps team at the chart review
impact: The chart values and the cache lifetime per environment; no business value changes

text: The seed job runs before the pods, the readiness probe reads the same check as the start-up check, and the three alerts are raised from the library's own metrics: a missing required value pages, a cache older than its time to live warns, and a failed refresh warns with the breaker state.
why: No source states the seed order, the probe or the alert thresholds, and without one order a service can start before the values it requires exist and serve traffic with nothing; the legacy story requires the refusal but not the mechanism.
read: RWB-E1-042 section 4 step 4, section 5 X3 and section 13 (parameter seed migration, ParameterStartupCheck as a health indicator); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 20 (/health and /metrics for the platform, every service)
confirm: Platform team, the DevOps team and the observability baseline owner at the SIT rehearsal
impact: The order of a release, the probe behaviour and the alert routes; no business value changes

why: Template and Rules section R3 puts parameters and reference data with P3 rwb-case by default ruling, and the Ownership Map assigns reference_version, reference_row and lov_value to P3; the platform library is not one of the 19 services and cannot own a schema, so the only consistent reading is that it reads and does not store.
